title: Cooperative Polygraphy

jokes.text: I wasn't prepared for a funeral with so much beeping.
jokes.setup: Pierce belonged to a 'weird, futuristic cult' (Laser Lotus), and they've just come from his funeral.
jokes.punchline: The specific absurd detail — that the funeral was notable not for grief but for 'so much beeping' — delivered with straight-faced resignation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold-open economy. The word 'beeping' does enormous work — it's specific, absurd, and tonally perfect for a sci-fi cult funeral. Jeff's detached delivery ('I wasn't prepared for') is very in-character. Strong opener.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So much beeping at a funeral.

jokes.text: Well, let's not judge. Everyone has a right to whatever fake religion they delusionally choose.
jokes.setup: Someone implies Pierce's cult is ridiculous.
jokes.punchline: Jeff frames tolerance as the value while simultaneously and completely undermining it by calling the religion 'fake' and its adherents 'delusional' in the same breath.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff Winger — performing open-mindedness while being maximally condescending. The contradiction is baked into a single sentence with great structural balance. 'Delusionally choose' is a lovely oxymoron. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: We shouldn't judge people for their beliefs. Everyone deserves acceptance and respect, no matter how different they are from us.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I mean, that's just fake and delusional, but I'm not judging.

jokes.text: ♪ Troy and Abed are in mourning ♪ / I don't think the audience got that we were singing 'mourning' with a 'u'.
jokes.setup: The Troy and Abed jingle is a beloved running gag. Here it's deployed at Pierce's funeral, causing discomfort. Abed then meta-comments that the wordplay (mourning/morning) was missed.
jokes.punchline: The pun reveal ('mourning with a u') is funny, but the deeper joke is that Abed is treating the funeral like a performance to be critiqued for craft and audience comprehension.
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered excellence. It subverts the beloved running gag by deploying it at a funeral (cringe), adds a wordplay layer with the 'mourning/morning' pun, and then has Abed break the fourth wall to critique the audience's ability to 'get' the joke. The meta layer is pure Abed characterization — he genuinely can't understand why people are upset about craft failure at a funeral. Earns the 8+ because it works on three levels simultaneously and is completely irreplaceable character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Good morning!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, we're at a funeral.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Good mourning.

jokes.text: You were singing 'mourning' with a 'u'? Oh, no.
jokes.setup: Abed reveals they meant the pun all along.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's horror is not about the funeral impropriety but about the pun itself — the pun was apparently WORSE than just doing the jingle at a funeral.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punchline payoff. 'Oh, no.' lands because it recontextualizes Jeff's objection entirely. Tight construction, great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you did the jingle during the eulogy?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We didn't know when else to do it!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's a funeral, Jeff. You don't perform a jingle at a funeral.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: In our defense, the timing seemed right at the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Right when they were lowering the casket?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We thought it was uplifting!

jokes.text: Once you reach level 16, you can see the color blurble.
jokes.setup: The group is reading the Laser Lotus theology pamphlet, trying to understand what happens to Pierce's 'life vapor.'
jokes.punchline: The invented word 'blurble' as a color only the enlightened can perceive — a perfect parody of cult theology and its unprovable, made-up rewards.
jokes.explanation: The invented word 'blurble' is genuinely funny — specific enough to feel real but nonsensical enough to highlight cult absurdity. Good economy. Slightly generic in terms of character specificity (anyone could read this).

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Do you think the audience will get the pun?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What pun?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've been saying 'cool. Cool cool cool' but I've been meaning to say 'cool. Cool cool cool' with a different emphasis.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, you've been singing 'cool cool cool'?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I've been singing 'Fool, fool, fool' the whole time.

jokes.text: If there is a blurble, the Lord keeps it hidden for a reason.
jokes.setup: Someone dismisses the cult theology as 'ridiculous cartoon nonsense.'
jokes.punchline: Shirley, a devout Christian, responds by treating blurble as a legitimate theological concept and incorporating it into her own religious framework — implying her God would suppress the cult's color.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Shirley characterization. She doesn't dismiss the cult on logical grounds but on theological ones — essentially arguing her God would have dominion over their fake color. The joke only works with Shirley and reveals her character beautifully: she takes all religious claims seriously, including absurd ones, because that's how deep her faith is. Very earned.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The made-up color 'blurble' is actually central to their theology. It represents the space between consciousness and reality.

jokes.text: No, Chang, our friend's funeral was not awesome. It was deeply sad. You know, funeral style.
jokes.setup: Chang bursts in and asks 'How was the funeral? Awesome?'
jokes.punchline: 'Funeral style' — Jeff's exasperated explanation that funerals are sad by definition, as if Chang needed the genre spelled out.
jokes.explanation: Functional. 'Funeral style' is a good tag that adds an extra beat. Jeff's weary condescension toward Chang is reliable character work, but nothing exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's ridiculous, I don't believe in any of that nonsense.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Although, you know, the Bible does mention blurble. It's right there in Deuteronomy.

jokes.text: All right, are you sure you guys aren't just doing the 'respect the dead' jig-a-lig?
jokes.setup: The group insists they genuinely mourn Pierce despite having complained about him constantly while alive.
jokes.punchline: Chang's invented phrase 'jig-a-lig' — casual and slightly nonsensical — to describe the social performance of post-mortem grief.
jokes.explanation: Chang's idiosyncratic vocabulary ('jig-a-lig') is a reliable character note. The observation about grief-performance is accurate and slightly pointed but not especially sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Was it awesome?

jokes.text: We complained about him when he was alive. This is different.
jokes.setup: Chang points out the group complained about Pierce constantly.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's completely logical but socially absurd distinction — complaints are time-stamped, death retroactively invalidates them. Delivered with zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Very economical and captures the group's self-delusion well. The unspoken logic (death = statute of limitations on grievances) is both funny and thematically true.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A funeral? Like, a funeral funeral? Funeral style?

jokes.text: Just a reminder you gotta live life to the fullest. By the time Pierce was my age, he had already been fired from 15 jobs. I've only seen two Police Academies. The last two.
jokes.setup: The group reflects solemnly on Pierce's death as a reminder to live fully.
jokes.punchline: Chang's metric for 'living fully' is: (1) being fired from 15 jobs, and (2) watching Police Academy films — but specifically only the worst two, the last two. The escalating wrongness is the joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: solemn life-lesson setup → Chang's genuinely unhinged yardstick for 'fullness' → the killer tag 'The last two' which makes it worse in every direction (he's not claiming quantity, just the objectively bad ones). Police Academy 7 and 8 are notoriously terrible. Pure Chang lunacy married to real comedic craft. Earns 8+ because the specificity ('the last two') elevates it from generic absurdism to precision-targeted absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You're all doing the jig-a-lig.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What's the jig-a-lig?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's that thing you do when you're pretending to be sad about something.

jokes.text: My name is Mr. Stone. / That's easy for you to say. / And for us to say.
jokes.setup: A mysterious man introduces himself as 'Mr. Stone' after the funeral.
jokes.punchline: Jeff notes 'Stone' is an easy name, Annie piles on — it's a quick silly joke about an obviously simple surname arriving with ominous gravitas.
jokes.explanation: Light wordplay, quick double-beat landing. Annie's echo ('And for us to say') adds a small extra laugh. Functional tension-breaker as the ominous stranger is introduced.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about Pierce and how he lived life to the fullest, you know? Just doing whatever he wanted, whenever he wanted. I think I should be more like that.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So I have a confession to make. I've watched all seven Police Academy movies. Not just watched them—I own them. On DVD. And I watch them constantly.

jokes.text: Aw, schnizzle. You guys are in trouble! / Mr. Chang, I presume. You're also listed as a suspect.
jokes.setup: Chang celebrates that the group is in trouble, preparing to leave.
jokes.punchline: He's also a suspect. His gleeful exit is immediately reversed.
jokes.explanation: Classic comic reversal. Chang's exit celebration is a solid setup for the trap. Good structure, 'schnizzle' is a fun Chang-ism.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Stone
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Mr. Stone.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's an unusually easy name to say.

jokes.text: We're losing Pierce! Everyone, quickly! / Someone get a balloon.
jokes.setup: An unrelated interlude — presumably Pierce's 'life vapor' in the energon pod is escaping, requiring urgent action.
jokes.punchline: The crisis response is 'get a balloon' — the most trivial, domestic object possible for what's being treated as an emergency.
jokes.explanation: Brief but effective absurdist beat. The energon pod introduced earlier pays off with a physical comedy bit — 'get a balloon' is funny because it's both logical (balloons trap air) and completely ridiculous in context.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh no, this is the best day of my life!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm a suspect? I'm outta here.

jokes.text: I always wanted to try a polygraph. They're like the pie fight of cop movies. Or the acupuncture of the legal system.
jokes.setup: The group reacts to being subjected to a lie-detector test.
jokes.punchline: Abed's two analogies are both structurally similar (beloved set-piece of a genre / questionable-but-fun alternative practice) but wildly different in register. The second one doesn't quite compute, which is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Very Abed — he processes everything through genre and media. 'Pie fight of cop movies' is a genuinely good line. The second analogy's slightly broken logic ('acupuncture of the legal system') is funny because it almost makes sense. Character-specific and inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I demand control of the study group!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Okay, fair enough.

jokes.text: Yeah, what a waste of murder. I mean, he was, like, 79.
jokes.setup: Someone says they can't believe Pierce thought they might murder him.
jokes.punchline: Jeff doesn't deny the possibility of murder — he objects to the efficiency of murdering someone who was about to die anyway.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and darkness. 'What a waste of murder' is a genuinely surprising and quotable construction — the word 'waste' applied to murder reframes killing as a resource allocation problem. Jeff doesn't even bother denying the murder impulse, just the ROI. This is sharp, dark, character-perfect (Jeff's amoral pragmatism), and laugh-out-loud surprising. Earns 8+ comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We need to call 911!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm calling them right now!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. I have a better idea.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Get a balloon.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A balloon? Someone's dying!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: A balloon always helps.

jokes.text: Have you ever had any thoughts of violence towards Pierce Hawthorne? — No. — Lie.
jokes.setup: The polygraph begins. Britta denies having violent thoughts about Pierce.
jokes.punchline: The machine immediately says 'lie' — confirming the obvious.
jokes.explanation: The first use of the polygraph punchline structure — sets up the repeating gag. Clean and functional. The humor is in how obvious the lie is.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: A polygraph is like a three-act structure for your nervous system. The setup is the control questions, the confrontation is the lie, and the resolution is when your palms get sweaty.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Or it's like a laugh track, but for guilt. It picks up on the audio cues your body's making when you're being dishonest.

jokes.text: In all your sexual fantasies about Pierce Hawthorne, none of them involved his murder?
jokes.setup: Britta clarifies she didn't murder Pierce, just wanted to slap him.
jokes.punchline: Stone pivots to asking about her sexual fantasies about Pierce — implying she has them — and then further implying murder might feature in those fantasies.
jokes.explanation: Double-layered offensiveness: first forcing the admission of sexual fantasies about Pierce (disgusting enough), then treating murder as a natural component of those fantasies. The question design is brilliantly structured to mortify. Very strong escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why would we murder Pierce? He's like 65 years old. We can just wait.

jokes.text: Are you gay? — No. — Are you sure you're not gay? — Yes. — Gay murderer says what? — What? — He's telling the truth. / I've been instructed to point out that that means you're gay.
jokes.setup: Jeff's turn. The first question is 'are you gay?' — a running theme in the show (Jeff's sexuality is frequently questioned/joked about).
jokes.punchline: The 'gay murderer says what' trap is a riff on 'blank says what.' Jeff says 'what,' confirming... something. Then Stone clarifies that him telling the truth (not being a gay murderer) means he IS gay. The logic is deliberately circular and absurd.
jokes.explanation: The 'gay murderer says what' gag is a clever structural trap — using Pierce's voice from beyond the grave to do what he always did in life (needle Jeff about his sexuality). The escalation from straight question to absurd word-trap to even more absurd 'logical' conclusion is well-constructed. Very Pierce-as-character.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So Pierce's final wish is... what exactly?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: He wants us to scatter his ashes at his favorite place.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's actually really sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Or he could wish for more wishes.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how final wishes work.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Technically, it could be.

jokes.text: Are you a dishonest person? — No. — She thinks that's true. / Uh, you could have just said no.
jokes.setup: Shirley denies being dishonest. The polygraph qualifies it as 'she thinks that's true' rather than confirming it.
jokes.punchline: The machine (or Stone) distinguishes between sincere self-deception and actual honesty. Shirley's self-image is intact but the audience knows better. Shirley then objects to the qualifier.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke about Shirley's consistent self-righteousness and limited self-awareness. 'She thinks that's true' is a genuinely clever polygraph modifier — distinguishing sincerity from truth. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Polygraph Examiner
dialogue.line: You ever cheat on a test?

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Polygraph Examiner
dialogue.line: You ever cheat on your partner?

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Polygraph Examiner
dialogue.line: Have you ever been sexually aroused by a member of your immediate family?

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: What?! No!

jokes.text: Is it true that you're a platinum level donor with the pro-life organization prenatalpatriots.org? ... It's my money. It's my choice. / Yeah, well, if I wanted the Government in my uterus, I'd fill it with oil and hispanic voters.
jokes.setup: Stone reveals Shirley secretly donates to a pro-life organization. Shirley responds with a pro-choice slogan reappropriated for pro-life. Britta fires back.
jokes.punchline: Britta's line about filling her uterus with oil and Hispanic voters is a hyperbolic political joke — over-the-top absurdist imagery that undercuts political discourse through sheer excess.
jokes.explanation: The joke does several things: Shirley's ironic use of pro-choice language for pro-life purposes reveals her obliviousness; Britta's response is perfectly in-character (over-the-top political, slightly unhinged), and the specificity of 'oil and Hispanic voters' is bizarre enough to be very funny. Strong character integration for both Shirley and Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: If a train leaves Chicago at 60 miles per hour and another train leaves Boston at 40 miles per hour, which one will reach the station first?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, obviously the one going 60 miles per hour.

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: Wrong. Neither one, because they're going in opposite directions.

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: Okay, here's another one. A man walks into a bar. What does he order?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A drink?

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: No, he orders a drink and a woman walks in. What does she order?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I don't know, what?

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: That means you're gay.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? That doesn't even make sense!

jokes.text: Keep it frosty, ladies. Don't let your goats get gotched.
jokes.setup: Shirley and Britta begin arguing about abortion politics.
jokes.punchline: Chang's invented idiom 'don't let your goats get gotched' — which appears to mean 'don't get riled up' — is entirely made-up and nonsensical.
jokes.explanation: Chang's self-invented vocabulary is a reliable source of laughs. 'Gotched' doesn't mean anything but sounds like it should, which is the fun.

dialogue.speaker: Polygraph Operator
dialogue.line: Your butt is a dork.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What?

jokes.text: D'oh! I meant to say, 'butts Carlton.' — He did mean to say, 'Butts Carlton.' — She said it.
jokes.setup: Troy is asked to state his name. He accidentally says his actual name, then 'corrects' himself to 'Butts Carlton,' and the polygraph confirms this was his intended answer.
jokes.punchline: Troy treats his real name as the mistake and 'Butts Carlton' as the intended answer. The polygraph validates his absurd internal logic.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Troy joke. The structure is impeccable: standard procedural moment (state your name) → Troy's childlike subversion → polygraph confirming his inner reality over external reality. 'She said it' as his only response to being verified is gold. The machine validating 'Butts Carlton' as his sincere intended name is an inspired twist on the polygraph premise. Earns 8+ for originality, structure, and irreplaceable character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My name is Troy. Troy Barnes.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Actually, it's Troy. T-R-O-I. No Y. Just kidding, there's a Y.

jokes.text: Did you get angry when Mr. Hawthorne told you Fat Albert died of diabetes? — Yes, like any American would.
jokes.setup: Stone asks if Troy was angered by Pierce's claim about Fat Albert.
jokes.punchline: 'Like any American would' — Troy treats outrage over a fictional cartoon character's fate as a universal, patriotic American response.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant in its simplicity. 'Like any American would' positions grief over a cartoon character as a civic duty. It's simultaneously perfect Troy characterization (his earnest, childlike pop culture reverence) and a sharp observation about collective nostalgia. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I have a doomsday plan. I've got a bunker with enough supplies for five years, a chest of gold coins, and a boat.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Why do you need a boat if you have a bunker?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: For when the bunker floods. And I've got condoms.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: For what, making water balloons?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: For bartering. Gold coins are great, but everyone wants condoms in the apocalypse. It's currency and protection.

jokes.text: Is it true that you and Abed Nadir have an elaborate doomsday escape plan to be used in the event of zombie attacks? ... We may have a designated rendezvous point and a couple of bugout bags filled with gold coins and condoms just in case we need to bargain our way onto a boat. The gold coins are for buying food.
jokes.setup: Stone asks about Troy and Abed's zombie apocalypse plan.
jokes.punchline: Troy's clarification — after listing gold coins AND condoms as bargaining chips for boat passage — that 'the gold coins are for buying food' implies the condoms have a different, unspecified bargaining function.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best. The clarification 'the gold coins are for buying food' is a masterclass in implication-by-omission. Troy never explains the condoms' function, which makes the audience's mind fill in the gap. The serious, matter-of-fact delivery of increasingly absurd contingency planning is perfectly Troy/Abed. The specificity (gold coins, condoms, boat) makes it feel like real planning rather than random absurdism. Earns 8+ comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Well, we could use them for water balloons.

jokes.text: Does your doomsday plan account for the welfare of any of your other friends? — Pass. — Answer the question. — No. — Troy! Rude! — It's a doomsday plan, not a picnic plan.
jokes.setup: The zombie plan is revealed to be exclusive to Troy and Abed.
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'It's a doomsday plan, not a picnic plan' — the most logical defense of selfishness imaginable, delivered without a trace of guilt.
jokes.explanation: The 'picnic plan' line is quotable, perfectly structured, and devastatingly logical within Troy's framework. His refusal to feel bad — trying 'pass' first, then owning it — builds the joke beautifully. The contrast of doomsday seriousness vs. 'picnic' casualness is a sharp juxtaposition.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Look, I didn't tell you guys because I was being merciful. You think I want to watch you suffer? I'm protecting you from disappointment.

jokes.text: Do you really wanna see the horrors we might have to endure just to get on a boat? — I guess not. — That's a lie.
jokes.setup: Troy defends the exclusivity of the doomsday plan by raising the horror of what survival might require.
jokes.punchline: Annie says 'I guess not' — and the polygraph calls it a lie. She actually DOES want to know. The machine reveals her morbid curiosity.
jokes.explanation: A clever use of the polygraph mechanic — it catches Annie in a socially acceptable lie that reveals a funny truth (she's morbidly curious about apocalypse horrors). Good structural use of the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm an open book. I have nothing to hide. I'm completely honest about everything.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I like watching cooking shows in my underwear and I cry at them.

jokes.text: Have you ever masturbated in the study room? [prolonged pause]
jokes.setup: Chang declares he has nothing to hide and is ready to 'deal out the truth.'
jokes.punchline: The question is immediately followed by a prolonged silence — the gap before the [05:33] timestamp suggests Chang's non-verbal response (combined with the audience's imagination) is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: Possibly the single biggest laugh in the episode. The 8-second gap before the next timestamp is the entire joke — Chang's silence (or expression, or non-answer) confirms everything. The setup ('nothing to hide') is a perfect ironic inversion. The question itself is sufficiently specific and gross to generate maximum cringe. The fact that this is never resolved with an explicit answer makes it funnier. Earns 8+ for structural elegance — the punchline IS the absence of a punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I have nothing to hide. Ask me anything.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay. What's your first name?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: ...Kevin.

jokes.text: Have you ever 9/11'd anyone?
jokes.setup: Abed's polygraph begins. The question is phrased as if '9/11' is a verb in common usage.
jokes.punchline: Treating the September 11th attacks as a replicable personal action — something a single person could do to another — is both absurdist and darkly subversive. It also quietly implies Pierce thought Abed might be a terrorist (connecting to his racism).
jokes.explanation: Four words, enormous impact. The joke works on multiple levels: Pierce's racism (Abed is Arab-American), the absurdity of using 9/11 as a verb, and the procedural normality with which it's asked. Exceptional economy — perhaps the most compressed joke in the episode. The lack of reaction is itself part of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So Abed, what happened with that girl you were talking to?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It didn't work out.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah? What happened, did she 9/11 you?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: ...Did you just use 9/11 as a verb?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Too soon?

jokes.text: When you were a child, did you ever kill a squirrel with a slingshot and was surprised that you felt nothing and wondered if you were capable of doing it to a human?
jokes.setup: Following the 9/11 question, Stone asks about Abed's childhood.
jokes.punchline: The question is an extremely specific psychopathic origin story — the classic 'animal cruelty as early sign of sociopathy' trope — asked in complete procedural seriousness. Abed's flat 'No' is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: The hyper-specificity of the question (squirrel, slingshot, feeling nothing) escalates the absurdity of Pierce's suspicion. It's funny because it's such a detailed accusation that also happens to describe textbook sociopathy origin stories from crime dramas.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, someone's been watching my Netflix account?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, they've been binge-watching everything. Lately it's been a lot of reality TV.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Reality TV? I don't watch reality TV.

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: That's because it wasn't you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well who was it?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We were kind of hoping you could tell us.

jokes.text: Do you and Troy still actively use Jeff's Netflix account without his permission? — Wait, what? — You told Pierce that? / You logged in at our place and never logged out, so we use it. / Is that why my review of The Grey is constantly changing? — Yes, stop giving it four stars. — I like Liam Neeson! — Then send him a message about the roles he chooses.
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy have been using Jeff's Netflix without permission.
jokes.punchline: The escalation: (1) unauthorized Netflix sharing, (2) the specific detail that Jeff's review of The Grey keeps being changed, (3) Jeff still defends his four-star review, (4) Abed's perfectly logical suggestion to contact Liam Neeson directly about his career choices instead.
jokes.explanation: The escalation is excellent — each line adds a new absurd detail. 'Send him a message about the roles he chooses' is the perfect Abed-logic conclusion: not 'stop reviewing his films' but 'contact the actor.' The choice of The Grey as the specific film Jeff over-rates is a nice real-world detail. Very character-specific to both Jeff's vanity and Abed's lateral thinking.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Troy, did you steal the Netflix password?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Jeff, I have to be honest with you. Liam Neeson's career peaked with Schindler's List. Everything after that has been a slow decline into straight-to-streaming action movies where he plays a guy with a very specific set of skills.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... not actually what I asked.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know, but someone needed to say it.

jokes.text: Miss Edison, did you use your exceptional intelligence and organizational skills to plot the foolproof murder of Pierce Hawthorne? — Aww! And no.
jokes.setup: Annie is asked if she murdered Pierce.
jokes.punchline: Before denying it, she pauses to appreciate being called exceptionally intelligent and organized — the flattery lands before the accusation registers. 'Aww! And no.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The construction is perfect: Pierce (through Stone) knows Annie well enough to soften a murder accusation with a compliment, and Annie is exactly the kind of person who would be momentarily charmed by it before catching herself. 'Aww! And no.' is a genuinely exceptional line — two syllables and a word capturing an entire character. Pure character comedy at its finest. Earns 8.5 easily.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me that someone in this study group has been stealing from Netflix this whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I can't believe it. After all these years, my personal mystery is finally solved.

jokes.text: Is it true that you overcharged Troy and Abed for their share of the rent? ... I padded your share of the rent by $10 and I've been putting it into a savings account that yields 4%. You'll be thanking me in six years when you find out you have $86.
jokes.setup: Annie is revealed to have been secretly overcharging her roommates.
jokes.punchline: Her justification is a forced savings account scheme — but the yield she describes is comically tiny: in six years, $10/month in savings at 4% compounds to exactly the $86 she names. The specificity of '$86' makes the math real and therefore funnier.
jokes.explanation: Annie's paternalism and financial hypercompetence are perfectly captured. The $86 figure rewards attentive viewers (the math actually works out roughly correctly over six years at 4%), which makes the joke both character-specific and cleverly grounded.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I may have made some questionable financial decisions with the study group's funds over the years.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: How questionable?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: After six years of careful investing and strategic planning, we've made a total return of... thirty-seven cents.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Thirty-seven cents?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pre-tax.

jokes.text: Oh, did you hear that, Abed? We've been washing paper plates and making our own toothpaste. But don't you worry. When we have robot bodies on the moon, we can share a free jacket.
jokes.setup: Troy learns he's been unknowingly forced to save money, while Annie justifies it as beneficial.
jokes.punchline: Troy's sarcastic vision of their future reward — robot bodies on the moon sharing one free jacket — is both a critique of Annie's paternalism and a perfect window into Troy's imagination.
jokes.explanation: The 'jacket money' callback escalates to 'one shared jacket on the moon with robot bodies.' The absurdist specificity of this dystopian sarcasm is very Troy — he goes full sci-fi to express a mundane complaint. Very quotable, very character-driven.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Eighty-six dollars? That's... that's a lot of money. I could buy 86 dollar cheeseburgers, or 172 fifty-cent tacos, or I could finally get that solid gold toilet seat I've had my eye on.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: A toilet seat isn't solid gold for eighty-six dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude.

jokes.text: Annie, you should know better than to horde money. That's a stereotype. / Was that anti-semitism? — No! That's sensitivity. It's anti-semitic to do things like that when you know full well you're Jewish.
jokes.setup: Shirley accuses Annie of hoarding money (a Jewish stereotype), then when called on it, claims NOT accusing Annie of hoarding was actually the anti-semitic thing.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's logic fully inverts: sensitivity to stereotypes is reframed as perpetuating them. It's both a parody of bad-faith identity politics reasoning AND perfect Shirley — she always finds a way to be right.
jokes.explanation: Shirley's rhetorical inversion is sharp and funny — it perfectly captures a certain kind of defensive social logic. The joke requires the audience to track the reversal, which rewards attention. Very character-specific to Shirley's self-justifying nature.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So Annie's been saving all our money? That's actually responsible.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Someone has to be. Do you know how much we spend on coffee?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's just survival. Without coffee, we'd have to face reality.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Exactly. Which is why I've also been rationing your meals.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: My meals? I thought I was just getting thinner from stress.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: At this rate, we'll have enough saved to buy a small island.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: An island? Annie, we can't even afford to leave the study room.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude. In five years, we'll be island people.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And in ten years we'll be gods worshipped by island natives who think we control the sun.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: See? This is why I save. For the sun-god years.

jokes.text: We could have bought a tire for our tire swing with that money. — Or your own Netflix account? — Liam Neeson? Not that great. — Your rating system is flawed.
jokes.setup: The group continues arguing about Annie's savings account.
jokes.punchline: The Netflix/Liam Neeson dispute resurfaces as a callback within the larger argument — everyone is now nursing their own grievance simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: A quick callback that keeps the Liam Neeson joke alive while adding a new complaint (tire swing). The layering of grievances is good ensemble writing. 'Your rating system is flawed' is a solid exit line.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm not hoarding money, I'm being fiscally responsible.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's what the Jewish people said, and look where that got them.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What? That doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Exactly. Antisemitism doesn't make sense either, but it's still a thing.

jokes.text: That completes the calibration round of questioning. We're ready to begin the formal inquest. / What do you mean, 'begin'?
jokes.setup: After all the revelations, Jeff tries to end the session, thinking it's over.
jokes.punchline: Stone reveals everything so far was just 'calibration' — the actual interrogation hasn't started. The ante is upped enormously.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom structure escalation used expertly. The reveal that Pierce has been warming up hits like a gut punch of dread/delight. Jeff's one-word response ('begin?') captures the horror perfectly. This is good structural comedy writing — the episode's midpoint stakes-raising moment.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Jeff, I've been thinking about your Netflix argument, and I have to tell you something. Your taste in shows is objectively worse than everyone else's in this study group.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You watch things ironically. You watch things because they're 'guilty pleasures.' You watch things that are just bad, Jeff. And you convince yourself you're being intellectual about it.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: The rest of us? We just like what we like. But you? You're up there doing this whole performance, and it's exhausting to watch.

jokes.text: Look, respect for the dead is only a thing because the dead usually don't do any more damage.
jokes.setup: Jeff argues they should stop the inquest out of respect for Pierce.
jokes.punchline: His own counterargument: respect for the dead is a convention based on their incapacity for harm — which Pierce is currently violating from beyond the grave.
jokes.explanation: One of Jeff's best lines in the episode. It's a genuinely original observation — the social contract of respecting the dead is reframed as a quid pro quo: they stop interfering, we stop mocking them. The fact that Pierce is actively breaking this contract makes the logic both funny and thematically resonant. Quotable, smart, and purely Jeff. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Clearly, Pierce is trying to lure us into a labyrinth of emotional manipulation and strategic instigation. And I think we're all smart enough to know we should quit while we're not ahead. — I do believe we should... — Yes, definitely. — Quit while we're ahead. — Absolutely. — Yep. — They're all lying. — We all know that, you judgmental bitch!
jokes.setup: Jeff makes an eloquent case for quitting, everyone agrees emphatically.
jokes.punchline: The polygraph calls them all liars. Britta's 'We all know that, you judgmental bitch!' — breaking the fourth wall of their own self-deception while also yelling at a machine — is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's comedic peaks. The setup is perfect: Jeff's self-aware speech about manipulation is itself part of the manipulation. Everyone lies in unison. The polygraph catches them all. And Britta — who cannot help herself — yells at the machine for saying what they already know. 'You judgmental bitch' directed at a polygraph machine is both funny and characterologically perfect (Britta calling out hypocrisy she's personally embodying). The structure — speech → agreement → mass lie detection → explosion — is flawless.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: It's not fake tofu, it's meatfu.

jokes.text: In order to save money, Shirley stopped using real tofu and replaced it with a midwestern tofu substitute called 'meatfu.' — Oh, my God! Oh! — It's still not actually meat... Legally.
jokes.setup: Britta is asked about Shirley's sandwich restaurant. Stone reveals a cost-cutting measure.
jokes.punchline: 'Meatfu' — the invented portmanteau of meat and tofu — is funny on its own. Shirley's desperate legal qualifier ('Legally') makes it land harder.
jokes.explanation: The word 'meatfu' is a genuinely good invention. The rhythm of Shirley's qualifier — 'It's still not actually meat... Legally.' — is perfect, with the pause before 'Legally' doing crucial work. It implies a previous legal determination that it's not meat, which suggests Shirley tested this in court (or was warned). Very Shirley — righteous entrepreneur corners.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: It's legally meat.

jokes.text: Did you know that Britta was high on marijuana at your son's baptism? — Well, no higher than usual. — Not true.
jokes.setup: Stone drops a bomb: Britta was high at a sacred religious ceremony.
jokes.punchline: Britta's defense — 'no higher than usual' — accidentally confirms she's usually high at church events, implying this is a baseline level of marijuana consumption for Britta in religious settings. Then the polygraph catches even this lowered bar as a lie.
jokes.explanation: The 'no higher than usual' construction is exceptional — it establishes a 'usual' level of church marijuana consumption as a normal baseline, which is both very funny and very Britta. The polygraph then immediately undermining even this lowered standard ('not true') is perfect escalation. This is calibrated character comedy — only Britta could say this.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I barely use drugs anymore!

dialogue.speaker: Polygraph Operator
dialogue.line: That's a lie.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, yeah, but not about the drugs.

jokes.text: No, I did drugs in the parking lot of your church. How else do you expect somebody to sit through something like that? At least with a bris there's an element of suspense.
jokes.setup: Britta defends doing drugs not IN the church but technically outside it.
jokes.punchline: The parking lot distinction as moral high ground, followed by the bris comparison — a bris involves an irreversible cutting, hence 'suspense' — as a reason baptisms need pharmaceutical enhancement.
jokes.explanation: Two great jokes in one breath. The parking lot technicality (Britta's signature bad-faith justifications) and 'at least with a bris there's an element of suspense' — which is both darkly funny (suspense = will they cut?) and a surprisingly sharp interfaith observation. 'Element of suspense' is a perfect, memorable phrase. Earns 8+ for the bris line alone, which is genuinely clever and surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, but circumcision has way more suspense. You don't know if the guy's going to mess up.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not the point of circumcision.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well it should be. Baptism is just dunking. Circumcision is like a thriller.

jokes.text: Well, next time, I'll have Cheech and Chong do the warm-up!
jokes.setup: Britta implies baptisms are boring without drugs.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's sarcastic suggestion to hire the most famous stoner comedians as church warm-up acts — delivered with Shirley's indignant righteousness.
jokes.explanation: Functional Shirley reaction — Cheech and Chong as the drug reference is a little dated and not particularly inventive, but Shirley's righteous delivery saves it.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well, maybe we should just have a drug-themed puppet show next Sunday. I'm sure that would really bring in the youth group.

jokes.text: Mr. Winger, is it true that you keep trophies of your sexual conquests? ... I have a box of forgotten items in my apartment. I happen to be a single male. Visitors leave things.
jokes.setup: Jeff is accused of keeping 'trophies' of sexual conquests.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's euphemism — 'forgotten items... visitors leave things' — is a masterpiece of technically-true denial. He's describing the same thing in the most blameless possible language.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jeff rationalization. 'Visitors leave things' is the most passive phrasing imaginable for what is clearly deliberate collection. The gap between 'trophies' and 'forgotten items' is the joke, and Jeff's confidence in the reframe is very in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A hawk came through my window and grabbed them right out of my hands. I've been keeping them as a reminder to always close my blinds.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, it happened!

jokes.text: Is one of your trophies a pair of Miss Perry's panties? — You told me a hawk stole them! — You exploited me and made me believe in a slightly more magical world.
jokes.setup: Stone reveals one of Jeff's 'trophies' belongs to Britta. She'd been told a hawk took them.
jokes.punchline: Britta's reaction — 'you made me believe in a slightly more magical world' — treats the lie about a hawk not as manipulative but as poetically robbing her of whimsy. This is a brilliant Britta line.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. 'You made me believe in a slightly more magical world' is completely unexpected — instead of being angry about the theft, Britta mourns the loss of the hawk fantasy. The word 'slightly' is doing immense work, keeping it grounded rather than fanciful. This is character writing at its best: the joke reveals something true and funny about Britta's character (she is a romantic despite herself). Highly quotable. Comfortably earns 8.5.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know what the worst part is? I actually believed in you. I thought you were different. But you're just like every other guy who's lied to me.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, come on—

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No. You had something special. You had this... magic. And you just threw it away for what? A quick con? Now every time I look at you, I'm just going to see the lie.

jokes.text: If you want to collect women's underwear, can't you just buy them? — They have to be won in battle.
jokes.setup: Shirley offers the logical alternative to stealing.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's completely serious framing of seduction as 'battle' and underwear as 'spoils of war' — delivered as if this is both obvious and honorable.
jokes.explanation: Four words that reveal everything about Jeff Winger's ego: 'won in battle.' The military framing of consensual sex as conquest is both funny and revealing — Jeff genuinely thinks of himself as a warrior. Extremely economical, perfectly in character, very quotable. Strong 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why do you have so many trophies?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: They're not trophies, Troy. They're conquests. Each one represents a battle won, a heart vanquished, a notch on my belt of romantic warfare.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's just... that's just sad, Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Sad? This is the spoils of victory. I'm a warrior, and these women are my fallen enemies.

jokes.text: Not really, Abed and I go through your stuff all the time. / Why do you keep bread in the freezer? / And why does your bathroom mirror say 'You're special' when you fog it up?
jokes.setup: Jeff objects to Pierce snooping through his things.
jokes.punchline: Troy and Abed casually reveal they also routinely invade Jeff's privacy, with two specific discoveries: frozen bread (eccentric) and the mirror message (deeply sad and revealing).
jokes.explanation: The bathroom mirror detail is devastating comedy. 'You're special' — written in what is clearly Jeff's own past self's attempt at daily affirmation — is both hilarious and genuinely poignant. It reveals that Jeff's bravado is compensating for profound self-doubt, and it's discovered by his friends who bring it up casually in a fight. The frozen bread is also funny (eccentric Jeff detail), but the mirror is the knife.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I was snooping through Jeff's apartment and I found this mirror with sticky notes all over it. Each one had something like 'You're a great person' and 'You deserve success.'

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not what that is.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude, it's okay. We all need a little help sometimes. I have affirmations too.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Those aren't affirmations, Troy. I wrote those to cover up the mirror because I couldn't stand looking at myself.

jokes.text: Okay! I did it! Okay? I killed Pierce! — Lie. — Okay, good. Just making sure.
jokes.setup: Troy is asked about his exclusive handshake with Abed.
jokes.punchline: In a panic about some question, Troy randomly confesses to murdering Pierce — the polygraph rejects it — and Stone calmly says 'just making sure.' The casualness of the check is funny.
jokes.explanation: Good bit — Troy's random false murder confession as an escape from the handshake question is very Troy (impulsive misdirection). Stone's 'just making sure' implies he treats spontaneous murder confessions as routine data points.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I killed a man.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm just testing the lie detector.

jokes.text: Mr. Barnes, did you invent that handshake? — Yes. — Lie.
jokes.setup: Troy claims ownership of the handshake.
jokes.punchline: The lie detector reveals he didn't invent it — which the following video clip confirms was stolen from a YouTube channel.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the YouTube reveal. Effective as a two-beat misdirection — the 'lie' lands as a tease before the punchline is fully delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Video
dialogue.line: Hey guys, what's up? So Troy Barnes has been stealing our sacred handshake. Don't forget to like and subscribe!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: THOU HAST BETRAYED ME! I SHALL SMITE THEE WHERE THOU STANDEST!

jokes.text: Hi, I'm Kevin, this is Kyle, and here's a fun handshake you can do with your best friend. All right! Thanks for watching, guys. Don't forget to rate us, comment, and subscribe.
jokes.setup: Stone plays a video blog to expose where Troy's handshake actually came from.
jokes.punchline: The handshake was stolen from a wholesome kids' YouTube channel hosted by 'Kevin and Kyle' — complete with standard YouTuber sign-off conventions.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the Troy/Abed handshake — a beloved symbol of their friendship — was just lifted from a YouTube tutorial is a genuinely funny deflation. 'Don't forget to rate us, comment, and subscribe' grounds it in recognizable internet culture.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: When someone betrays you, you're supposed to feel hurt, angry, maybe seek revenge. It's the classic three-act structure of betrayal.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But I've watched enough TV to know that if I just accept it and move on, I become the more evolved character. So I'm going to subvert your expectations and be weirdly okay with this.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Which means you don't get the satisfaction of my pain, making you the real loser in this narrative.

jokes.text: Can't look at you right now. — Then you should know I'm crying.
jokes.setup: Abed is devastated by the handshake revelation.
jokes.punchline: Abed says he can't look at Troy — Troy immediately exploits this to claim he's crying in a way Abed can't verify.
jokes.explanation: Economical and sweet. Troy immediately gaming the unverifiable crying claim is both funny and oddly moving — his attempt at emotional manipulation as a form of affection is very Troy. Great line economy.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm not going to fall into the emotional pattern this time. I'm going to stay detached and—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: ...I'm already doing it, aren't I?

jokes.text: I forgive you, but only to escape the established pattern of self-righteous indignation followed by immediate comeuppance.
jokes.setup: Abed is asked to forgive Troy for the handshake theft.
jokes.punchline: Abed recognizes they're in a sitcom narrative loop (grievance → righteousness → humiliation) and chooses forgiveness as a tactical escape from the pattern — not out of genuine feeling.
jokes.explanation: Pure Abed at his most meta. He identifies the narrative pattern (self-righteous indignation → comeuppance) as a recognizable loop and opts out of it via forgiveness — not because he forgives Troy but because he wants to skip the structural beat. This is exactly the kind of meta-awareness the show is known for. The line is long but every word earns its place. Only Abed can say this. Earns 8.5 for concept and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, you're tracking all of us? That's insane!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's not insane. The government does it, Facebook does it, your phone does it. I'm just being honest about it.

jokes.text: Mr. Nadir. — Okay, I guess it's happening anyway. — You broke my heart. Continue.
jokes.setup: Despite Abed's pre-emptive forgiveness, the polygraph continues to reveal his misdeeds.
jokes.punchline: Abed acknowledges his attempt to escape the narrative loop failed ('happening anyway'), then pivots immediately to genuine grievance performance ('you broke my heart') followed by a curt 'Continue' — suggesting he's embracing the structure now that it's inevitable.
jokes.explanation: Perfect follow-through on the previous joke. 'I guess it's happening anyway' is both resignation and acceptance. 'You broke my heart. Continue.' is a great rhythmic line — the word 'Continue' reframes the heartbreak as something to be processed and moved past in real-time.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I was just thinking... we won't need to track Pierce anymore.

jokes.text: Is it true that you planted geo-trafficking devices on everyone in the group so that you would know where they are at all times? — Yes. / Okay, you guys are changing your faces. Are you mad at me or hungry?
jokes.setup: Abed admits to tracking everyone. The group reacts with visible upset.
jokes.punchline: Abed reads their facial expressions and genuinely cannot distinguish anger from hunger — either he has limited emotional processing or he's so unsurprised by his own behavior that he's genuinely confused about their reaction.
jokes.explanation: The 'mad or hungry' question is a great Abed line — it treats two very different emotional states as equivalent ambiguous signals. The deadpan delivery of a surveillance admission followed immediately by genuine confusion about facial expressions is very strong Abed characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: She's created her own language. Watch this. Hey Abed, you're a bloggity blarghnaxian!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know you are, but what am I?

jokes.text: Because we already live in a totalitarian surveillance state. Do you not read my status updates?
jokes.setup: Someone objects to Abed's surveillance.
jokes.punchline: Britta objects to being tracked not on privacy grounds but because she's already protesting government surveillance and Abed should know this from her social media posts — which is itself a form of surveillance.
jokes.explanation: Classic Britta — she objects to surveillance while expecting people to monitor her surveillance-protest status updates. The self-undermining circularity is very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I created a fake boyfriend because I wanted to see if I could manipulate everyone's emotions by manufacturing a false narrative of personal growth.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And it worked perfectly until you all decided to care about my actual well-being instead of just enjoying the story I was telling.

jokes.text: It's cool. When one of you gets kidnapped, you'll be glad you don't have to count the bumps on the highway from the trunk of the car.
jokes.setup: The group objects to being tracked.
jokes.punchline: Abed's justification is that they might get kidnapped, and tracking them preemptively helps avoid the classic kidnapping navigation technique (counting highway bumps from a trunk) — delivered with complete confidence and pragmatism.
jokes.explanation: The 'counting bumps from the trunk' detail is specific enough to suggest Abed has thought about kidnapping scenarios in detail (probably from crime movies). His framing of surveillance as a friend-protection service is both touching and deeply unsettling. Very Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you created a fake boyfriend?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He's a sommelier from Portland who does CrossFit and makes artisanal cheese.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's... incredibly specific.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He also has strong opinions about craft beer and volunteers at a pottery studio on weekends.

jokes.text: Are those blinking dots us? — Mm-hmm. — Well, what's this one all the way to the side? — That's where Pierce is buried.
jokes.setup: The group examines Abed's tracking map on a device.
jokes.punchline: One of the tracked dots is Pierce's burial site — Abed has been tracking the dead body. The morbidity lands as a sudden dark turn.
jokes.explanation: The reveal is perfectly timed and perfectly economical. The setup (blinking dot on a map) has a clear innocent explanation, then the dark twist arrives with no preamble. 'That's where Pierce is buried' delivered matter-of-factly is a great dark punchline. The subsequent clarification (he was trying to retrieve the expensive tracker from the coffin) makes it even better — Abed's concern is pragmatic, not morbid.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Oh, you want to go there? Fine. Troy, you cry during insurance commercials. Jeff, you practice your 'serious face' in the mirror. Britta, you still sleep with a nightlight. Annie, you alphabetize your highlighters by shade. Shirley, you've named all your cleaning supplies. And Pierce... well, Pierce, you Google yourself every morning and read the comments out loud to your cat.

jokes.text: Is that why you were spending so much time by the coffin? — I was trying to get it back. They're expensive. And he's not moving anymore.
jokes.setup: Callback to the opening scene — Abed was noted to be lingering at the coffin.
jokes.punchline: 'He's not moving anymore' — Abed's matter-of-fact observation that a dead man won't return a tracker recontextualizes his funeral behavior as logistics management.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the episode's opening pays off beautifully. What seemed like grief was inventory management. 'He's not moving anymore' as a reason a dead person can't return equipment is both very dark and perfectly Abed-logical. Earns 8+ for the callback structure and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I lied on the polygraph. I'm not actually a real changlourious being.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm not even a real person. I'm a sentient pile of fears and insecurities held together by a desire to seem cool.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Also, I've been stealing from the vending machines.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: And I may have faked my entire academic record.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I don't even know what my real name is anymore.

jokes.text: If you makes you feel any better, you'll never find them.
jokes.setup: The group asks where Abed planted the tracking devices on their bodies.
jokes.punchline: Instead of revealing the locations, Abed offers the consolation that they can't find them — framing inaccessibility as comfort.
jokes.explanation: Very Abed — his attempt at reassurance is actually more alarming than the original revelation. 'You'll never find them' as a comforting thought is perfect Abed-logic humor.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I've been going into the study room when no one's around.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: At first it was just in the study room.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Then it was in the hallways.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Then it was in the cafeteria.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Now it's everywhere.

jokes.text: Miss Edison, is it true you once secretly dosed the members of your study group with a pharmaceutical amphetamine? ... I put 5 milligrams of something-something in your coffees and we all got an 'A.'
jokes.setup: The polygraph reveals Annie secretly drugged everyone to pass an exam.
jokes.punchline: 'Something-something' — Annie's euphemism for the specific drug she used, suggesting she knows exactly what it was but is unwilling to name it. The casualness of the admission is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The 'something-something' is a brilliantly evasive euphemism. Annie's self-justification ('we all got an A' as if that settles it) is very character-specific. The juxtaposition of her sweetness with actual drug-spiking is a great escalation of the Annie character — she really will cross any line in pursuit of academic achievement.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Honesty is the foundation of all meaningful relationships. When we strip away pretense and embrace truth, we create genuine human connection. It's not just morally right—it's fundamentally practical.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, I've been honest my whole life, and look at me—I'm loaded.

jokes.text: I'm a bad person for tracking your location, but you altered my brain chemistry? I was up for three days that week. I invented an entire language, you fliztbarping gitzgorg.
jokes.setup: Abed reacts to learning Annie dosed him.
jokes.punchline: 'Fliztbarping gitzgorg' — Abed curses Annie in the language he invented while high on amphetamines, the existence of which proves how seriously the drugs affected him.
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in the episode. The setup is established (Abed was up 3 days on amphetamines, invented a language) and the PUNCHLINE is Abed using the invented language as a curse word right now, in the conversation. It's constructed brilliantly: tell the audience you invented a language → immediately demonstrate it by insulting Annie in that language. 'Fliztbarping gitzgorg' is phonetically perfect (sounds like actual swearing). The structure is flawless, it's completely irreplaceable Abed characterization, and it's a genuine surprise. This is the episode's crown jewel. Comfortably at the top of the scale.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I have a confession to make. I've been lying to all of you. I'm not actually as smart as I pretend to be. I'm just really good at sounding smart. And honestly? I'm okay with that because it means you all think I'm amazing, which is what really matters.

jokes.text: You're Olympic pole-vaulting hopeful Brent Underjaw?
jokes.setup: Jeff is revealed to have catfished Annie with a fake profile.
jokes.punchline: The name 'Brent Underjaw' — specific, slightly ridiculous, implying a prominent jaw — and the very specific fake identity (Olympic pole-vaulting hopeful) make the catfish both funnier and sadder.
jokes.explanation: 'Brent Underjaw' is a name crafted for maximum comedy: it sounds vaguely plausible but 'Underjaw' is a word that only exists in anatomy to describe a mandible. 'Olympic pole-vaulting hopeful' adds specificity that implies Jeff chose the most aspirational-but-achievable fake identity he could. Very quotable. The name alone gets a huge laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I hit a car in the parking lot and I didn't leave a note.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: But that's not even the worst part. At the improv class I took, I did a sketch where I played a stereotypical Asian character with a terrible accent.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: And everyone laughed! They thought it was hilarious! I felt so guilty I came here to confess.

jokes.text: I noticed whenever you were in a relationship, you hummed a lot and made pancakes in the morning. / It wasn't about hurting you. I did what I did in the name of breakfast.
jokes.setup: Jeff explains why he catfished Annie.
jokes.punchline: 'I did what I did in the name of breakfast' — Jeff frames a manipulative fake relationship as an act of altruism motivated by Annie's pancake-making habits.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. 'In the name of breakfast' is an absurd and perfect justification for catfishing — Jeff's self-interest is disguised as concern for Annie, but the real motivation is revealed to be pancakes. The specific details (humming, pancakes) make it feel specific and real. 'In the name of breakfast' is an instantly quotable, hall-of-fame-level phrasing. This line alone would justify watching the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I lied about going to Legoland. I've never been to Legoland. I just said that to seem cool.

jokes.text: I bore my soul to you! I told you about my holding hands at Disneyland fantasy.
jokes.setup: Annie is devastated that she shared intimate dreams with a fake person.
jokes.punchline: Her deepest romantic fantasy is... holding hands at Disneyland. The wholesome specificity is both funny (how modest the fantasy is) and touching.
jokes.explanation: Annie's most secret desire being to hold hands at Disneyland is exactly right for her character — earnest, slightly childlike, wholesome to a fault. The specificity earns the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I know I have a problem with passive-aggression. I'm working on it.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Here, I baked you a cake. It's not poisoned or anything. Well, it's not poisoned.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: See? I did it again.

jokes.text: Jeff made me apply for handicapped parking so he can get a better spot. / Britta's the one that invited Garrett to Annie's birthday party! / Troy won't sit on a toilet seat after Jeff! / When we're alone, Shirley refers to you guys as 'those people.' / When Annie's with other females, dude, she calls Jeff her uncle! / Shirley thinks we're all going to hell! — You are all going to hell!
jokes.setup: Following Annie's challenge ('Do you care about people at all, Abed?'), Abed detonates the entire group by rapid-fire revealing everyone's secret betrayals.
jokes.punchline: The cascade of accusations escalates to Shirley's theological verdict — 'You are all going to hell!' — which is both a confession (she does think this) and a perfectly in-character response to public exposure.
jokes.explanation: One of the great ensemble comedy sequences in the episode. Each reveal is calibrated to its character: Jeff's parking scam (selfish status anxiety), Britta inviting Garrett (mischievous chaos), Troy's toilet phobia about Jeff (childish hierarchy), Shirley's 'those people' (her barely-hidden superiority), Annie calling Jeff her uncle (maintaining distance), Shirley's damnation verdict (genuine religious belief and self-righteousness). The structure — rapid fire confessions → Shirley's escalation → Shirley confirming it — is structurally near-perfect. Earns 8.5 for sustained excellence across the whole sequence.

jokes.text: Mr. Hawthorne hasn't asked a question in quite some time, Mr. Winger.
jokes.setup: Jeff tells everyone to stop letting Pierce do this to them.
jokes.punchline: Stone's quiet correction that Pierce hasn't been asking questions — the chaos just came from the group itself — reframes Pierce's absence as a dramatic reveal. The characters have been weaponizing each other without help.
jokes.explanation: One of the most structurally important lines in the episode — it functions as the thematic punchline to the entire first act. The comedy lies in the quiet deflation: the group was blaming Pierce for the chaos, but they did it all themselves. Stone's matter-of-fact delivery makes it devastating. High craft score for structural significance and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Britta, in my will, I've arranged for my sperm to be preserved in perpetuity.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What? Pierce, no!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Yes! I'm going to create an army of geniuses. Little Pierces running around, changing the world.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's insane. That's absolutely insane.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Is it? Or is it the only sane thing I've ever done?

jokes.text: I didn't just masturbate in the study room. I masturbated everywhere. Everywhere!
jokes.setup: In a moment of cathartic group confession, Chang follows up on the earlier unanswered polygraph question.
jokes.punchline: Chang's confession escalates from the specific ('study room') to the universal ('everywhere') — shouted twice, as if volume conveys pride rather than shame.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the best awkward silence earlier in the episode. 'Everywhere. Everywhere!' is genuinely hilarious — the repetition with escalating emphasis turns confession into a declaration. Chang's pride in his own pervasiveness is a perfect character note. This is a great callback landing on a crowd-pleasing button. The two-word repeated punchline is as economical as it gets.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Annie, I want you to have this tiara. It belonged to my mother.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh Pierce, that's so sweet!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, she won it in a beauty pageant in 1952. Back then, if you didn't win, they'd publicly humiliate you. She came in second. The judges said her smile was 'too eager.' She never smiled again.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's... that's horrible.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I know. So I want you to have it, as a reminder that beauty pageants destroy souls.

jokes.text: Confession is good for the soul. You should try it sometime.
jokes.setup: Chang's graphic confession has just scandalized the room.
jokes.punchline: Shirley responds to Chang's masturbation omnibus with religious encouragement for more confession — missing the irony that more details from Chang would be worse, not better.
jokes.explanation: Functional Shirley beat. The religious framework applied to a deeply inappropriate confession is reliable Shirley comedy, though not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I got you something special, Jeff. A bottle of the finest brandy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, this is... wait, what is this?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It's not just any brandy, Jeff. It's been aged for 20 years in oak barrels.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, that sounds nice actually.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: With a special ingredient I added myself.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What kind of ingredient?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Let's just say it came from a very happy place.

jokes.text: I'm Jeff Winger, and if I had my choice, I would rather look at myself naked than the women I sleep with.
jokes.setup: In a moment of cathartic honesty, the group volunteers confessions.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's confession is not a moral failing but a vanity confession — he is more attracted to his own body than to his partners. It's both very Jeff and genuinely surprising.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jeff confession — it reveals his narcissism as his actual flaw rather than the more conventional ones we might expect. The specificity ('rather look at myself naked') is bold and completely in-character. The formal 'I'm Jeff Winger, and...' framing adds comedic gravity. Earns 8+ for precision character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: Pierce bequeaths to Jeffrey Winger his entire collection of premium spirits and rare alcohols, totaling approximately $47,000 in value.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wow, that's... actually really generous.

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: However, there is a condition. The will states: 'Only to be consumed in the company of good friends, or in moments of genuine despair.' Additionally, Pierce notes: 'And should Jeffrey ever run out, he knows where to find more of my special homemade brew.'

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What's his special homemade brew?

dialogue.speaker: Stone
dialogue.line: It simply says here: 'My essence.'

jokes.text: I'm the one who hit Jeff's Lexus in the parking lot. It wasn't a taco truck, and it was racist of me to improvise such an ethnically specific vehicle.
jokes.setup: Britta confesses to hitting Jeff's car.
jokes.punchline: The racism isn't the act (hitting the car) but the cover story she invented — a taco truck, which is an ethnically coded vehicle she reached for instinctively. She calls herself out for it.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Britta joke. The double confession — hitting the car AND the racism of her lie — is brilliantly structured. 'Ethnically specific vehicle' is a perfect phrase. The joke works because Britta is a character who considers herself above racism but keeps accidentally revealing unconscious biases. It's both funny and cutting. Earns 8.5 for the layered self-awareness that is simultaneously self-incriminating.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, that's it? That's all you're giving me?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Troy, it's a sperm sample. What were you expecting?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I don't know, I just thought... I mean, I've been saving up for this moment my whole life, and it's in a cup the size of a shot glass?

jokes.text: I only give money to homeless people when I'm walking with someone.
jokes.setup: Confessions continue.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's admission that his charity is entirely performative — he only gives when witnessed — is a sharp observation about social signaling in charitable giving.
jokes.explanation: Very economical and very true. It's a universally relatable admission delivered as a confession, which makes it hit harder. Pure Jeff characterization — he's not even ashamed, just honest.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: The honest prioritization of money over personal growth

jokes.text: I've never been to Legoland. I just wanted you guys to think I was cool.
jokes.setup: Confessions continue.
jokes.punchline: Troy has apparently referenced Legoland repeatedly as a credibility-booster — now revealed as a lie. The assumption that Legoland attendance confers coolness is very Troy.
jokes.explanation: Troy using Legoland as a cool-kid status symbol is perfect Troy characterization. The gap between how childlike the aspiration is and how earnest his confession is makes this funny and slightly heartbreaking.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Cool. Cool cool cool cool cool cool cool.

jokes.text: I can be passive-aggressive sometimes. Don't everybody disagree at once. Oh, Lord, I did it again.
jokes.setup: Shirley confesses to passive-aggression.
jokes.punchline: She immediately demonstrates it ('Don't everybody disagree at once') and then catches herself doing it again mid-confession.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode, possibly the most structurally elegant. The confession PROVES ITSELF in real time — she states the flaw, demonstrates it, then self-aware catches herself, which itself has a passive-aggressive edge ('Oh, Lord, I did it again'). It's a Möbius strip of character comedy. The structure is perfect: statement → immediate live demonstration → meta-awareness → implicit continuation. Only Shirley can deliver this. Earns high 8+ comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Death by excessive masturbation for the sperm cylinders

jokes.text: When any of you chew gum, I want to punch you. You may as well have submachine guns in your mouths. It vibrates my skull.
jokes.setup: Confessions continue. Abed's turn.
jokes.punchline: Abed's confession is a sound-sensitivity rant — characteristically precise and unexpectedly violent ('submachine guns in your mouths'). The escalation from 'want to punch' to 'submachine guns' to 'vibrates my skull' is very Abed.
jokes.explanation: Very Abed — his confessions involve precise sensory observations rather than moral failures. 'Submachine guns in your mouths' is a memorably excessive image for chewing. The tone is clinical and furious simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Finally learning how Pierce died

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: He died from dehydration while producing sperm samples

jokes.text: Britta Perry... Do you know that you hate yourself more than you should and that your passion inspired me? — No. — That's true. She didn't know. / To Miss Perry, I leave my iPod Nano filled with music to take life less seriously by.
jokes.setup: Pierce's final questions shift from interrogation to genuine feeling — first revealing what he actually thought of each person.
jokes.punchline: The warm sentiment is immediately followed by Pierce's gift: an iPod Nano (outdated by this point) with curated party music. The sincerity-to-gadget gap is funny. Also the polygraph confirming Britta genuinely didn't know Pierce cared is touching and funny.
jokes.explanation: The pivot to Pierce's genuine feeling is well-handled, and the iPod Nano as a gift (already becoming dated) is a lovely Pierce-specific touch — he's trying to be cool but his frame of reference is slightly off.

jokes.text: I also leave you this liquid nitrogen cooled cylinder of my hyper-virile sperm in case your lesbian lifestyle one day wears out and you wish to raise an army of geniuses.
jokes.setup: Following a touching bequest, Stone reads Pierce's addendum gift.
jokes.punchline: The 'liquid nitrogen cooled cylinder of hyper-virile sperm' as a bequest — with the specific justification about 'lesbian lifestyle wearing out' and 'army of geniuses' — is an extraordinary combination of Pierce's racism, sexism, narcissism, and backhanded affection.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Pierce-from-beyond-the-grave characterization. The sperm bequest is designed to be offensive in a very specific Pierce way: it manages to be homophobic, presumptuous, and narcissistic all at once — but with a weird underlying affection ('hyper-virile' as a compliment he's giving Britta). The 'army of geniuses' detail is the peak — Pierce's megalomania knows no bounds. This becomes a running gag throughout the final act.

jokes.text: Where she can take What's-his-name and however many children she has now.
jokes.setup: Pierce bequeaths a timeshare to Shirley.
jokes.punchline: Pierce can't remember Shirley's husband's name or how many children she has — 'What's-his-name' and 'however many children she has now' revealing his fundamental inattention despite claiming to respect her.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Pierce characterization — he genuinely respects Shirley but doesn't pay attention to the people around her. The juxtaposition of 'credit to our species' with not knowing her husband's name is very funny.

jokes.text: Also sperm. / Jeff Winger, did you know you're gay? — No. — Agree to disagree.
jokes.setup: The sperm bequest recurs for Shirley, then the gay question surfaces again.
jokes.punchline: The polygraph's 'Agree to disagree' — instead of the standard 'lie' or 'truth' — is a novel modifier that implies the machine itself acknowledges this is a matter of ongoing dispute rather than fact.
jokes.explanation: The 'agree to disagree' evolution of the polygraph's gay-question response is a great escalation on the running gag.
